correctness.rationale: The multiplicity convention gives complete additivity of S. For t≥2, induction under t=ab with a,b≥2 proves S(t)≤a+b≤ab=t, with prime cases immediate; S(1)=0. If composite m=ab satisfies S(m)=m−1, then (a−1)(b−1)≤2, so 2≤a≤b leaves only (2,2),(2,3). The first gives S(4)=4, the second S(6)=5. If n+1 is prime then S(n+1)=n+1>S(n), even at n=1. Otherwise a prime member must be n, and the lemma forces n+1=6, with S(5)=S(6)=5. This works for neighbors of arbitrary factorization complexity. The smallest-prime-factor checker ranges only through 2000000; the two finite predicates corroborate but do not establish exhaustiveness over all m or n. No fresh execution or formal verification is claimed.
residual_risks: The result makes no claim about general composite-only pairs or either member being a higher prime power.

value.rationale: This is the complete minimal prime-factor layer on either side of a standard consecutive-factor-sum equation. Unlike a census or the different two-sided low-Ω problem, it rules out every composite neighbor of arbitrary complexity except the lone witness. Its exact one-below lemma isolates the obstruction and is independently reusable when comparing S(m) to a nearby prime, without making a claim about infinitude or higher-complexity pairs.
residual_risks: The value is a complete, narrow classification, not an improvement to global bounds or a general solution to the Ruth–Aaron problem.
